name: Wig (lace front)

lead: A lace front wig has a thin, skin-toned mesh at the front with hairs tied in by hand, so the hairline appears to grow from the skin. The payoff is an instant full head of hair, used for fashion and to conceal hair loss, including medical hair loss.

The lace blends with the skin at the hairline, and the hair is attached by pins, elastic or skin-safe adhesive. It works while worn and is removable; no trial has tested lace fronts specifically. In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, lace fronts are discussed mainly as a way to conceal hairline loss.

paras: People choose full-lace or partial-lace versions in French or Swiss lace, trim the lace to the hairline, and secure it with pins, elastic or adhesive. They maintain it like hair with regular care and replace it as it wears.
Adhesives and tight attachment can irritate the scalp. Cost and replacement needs vary with materials. Wigs are not regulated as drugs.

chain: Hair covers thin or bald areas
angle.text: A lace front wig gives a full head of hair with a hairline that appears to grow from the skin, visible the moment it is worn. It is removable and used to conceal hairline loss.

lead: A lace front wig is a wig whose front hairline is made from a sheer, skin-toned lace panel into which individual hairs are tied by hand, so the hair appears to emerge from the skin.[1][2] It gives a full head of hair and a natural-looking hairline immediately, which is why it is used by people with receding hairlines, thinning or baldness as well as for fashion, theatre and protective styling.[1][2]

Two main types exist. A lace front has lace only along the front hairline with a sturdier material elsewhere, and is the more common; a full lace wig has a lace base across the whole piece, which allows high ponytails, updos and parts anywhere.[1] The wearer can choose the hairline shape and part freely, and many pieces include fine 'baby hair' at the temples to hide the lace edge.[1] Hair is human or synthetic, with density expressed as a percentage, where 130% and 150% are popular and higher density costs more.[1]

Wearers attach the lace with glue or tape applied along the hairline, pressing the lace onto the dried adhesive; pieces can stay on for weeks with regular washing and styling, and can be worn for swimming and exercise.[1] Wigs more broadly are worn by people with medical hair loss, most often chemotherapy patients and people with alopecia areata.[2] No clinical trial specific to lace front wigs has been found; they are a cosmetic covering rather than a treatment.
infobox: Glue or tape along the hairline; pins or elastic[1][2]

paras: Wigs are built from human hair, animal hair such as horse, goat or yak, or synthetic fibre.[2] Human hair of the best grade is unbleached, uncoloured and kept with its cuticles aligned, often marketed as Remy hair; synthetic fibre has no grain direction and is made in fixed colours.[2] Construction uses either silk-thread wefts sewn to a net foundation or individual strands hand-knotted onto a foundation.[2]

In a lace front, each strand of the front edge is knotted into a lace panel so the hairline resembles natural growth.[1][2] Lace is preferred because its flesh tone is close to invisible against the skin, although lace front wigs can look obviously like wigs when the hair is pulled back.[1]

Wigs have a long history. A statue of Princess Nofret wearing a wig dates to roughly 2613 to 2494 BC, Egyptians wore them to shield shaved heads from the sun, and European men wore wigs as standard dress in the 17th and 18th centuries.[1][2] A hand-knotting method using a ventilating needle began replacing the older weft method in the 1800s, and by the 1870s machine-made lace had made lace bases affordable and popular.[1] Synthetic modacrylic wigs from the 1960s made wigs cheaper.[2]

Lace wigs are described as a non-surgical option for people experiencing hair loss.[1] In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities they are discussed mainly as a way to restore a hairline without treatment or surgery, and as a fallback while other approaches are tried.

Adhesives and tight attachment are the main practical considerations. Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by chronic pulling force, and encyclopedic sources list hairpieces and wigs, particularly where braids are tightened under them during frequent reattachment, among the causes, along with tight braids, extensions and headgear.[3] A 2022 case report in the British Journal of Dermatology described leucoderma, a loss of skin pigment, secondary to wig wearing.[4] Historically, wigs could harbour lice.[2]
